newsitem.title: REPUBLIC OF IRELAND: Ireland creates 1,200 jobs, says more on way.
newsitem.headline: Ireland creates 1,200 jobs, says more on way.

text.p: The Irish government announced the creation of more than 1,200 new jobs on Wednesday and made an election-year boast that it was trimming the unemployment rolls by a thousand people a month.

The announcement was made amid speculation that Prime Minister John Bruton would call an early general election next month and use job creation as a major reason that voters should return his left-right coalition to power.

His brother, Enterprise and Employment Minister Richard Bruton said in a statement that the government's investment arm, IDA Ireland, had secured 1,249 new jobs with 17 grant-aided projects across the country.

"As we conclude the first quarter of the year, I am particularly pleased that job creation in companies supported by IDA Ireland remains bouyant and companies are recruiting at about the same pace as 1996, the best job creation year ever."

Foreign investors, attracted by 10 percent corporation tax, skilled workers and EU and government grants, have poured into Ireland, trimming the unemployment rate from 13 to 11 per cent in recent years.
Bruton said: "On average over 1,000 new jobs a month are now being created in these companies."
He unveiled a series of new projects, some of which had assistance from the European Union, to create jobs in a variety of enterprises from language schools to computer software.
"The focus in the Dublin projects, with 620 new jobs, is primarily on people-based, value-added services such as software, back office and customer support services," he said.
"At the regional locations, where there are 629 new jobs, the employment opportunities encompass engineering and electronics, as well as software."

The government must hold a general election no later than November this year but it is widely expected to cash in on the biggest tax give-away Irish budget in history and call the poll before the end of June.

The government is riding the crest of a wave of economic success which has propelled Ireland into the top league of fastest-growing economies in Europe. Its seven per cent rate of growth is double that of most major economies.
The Prime Minister may announce a date this month when parliament resumes after the Easter recess, but the main opposition party, Fianna Fail, has already put its campaign apparatus into battle gear.
Thousands of posters showing Fianna Fail leader Bertie Ahern have gone up on hoardings across the country and spokesmen are targeting a worrying drug problem as an election issue.

The coalition government, which groups Bruton's Fine Gael, Labour party and Democratic Left, says it has built more prison places and attacked narcotics traffic with unprecedented firmness by confiscating the assets of suspected suppliers.

Ahern's Fianna Fail party led the last government but it collapsed under the then prime minister, Albert Reynolds, in a scandal over delays in extraditing a paedophile priest from British-ruled Northern Ireland.
